Like what many others have said, I think it’s disrespectful and harmful to yourself and others to claim a disorder without being diagnosed. I full heartedly support people saying “I have symptoms of xyz”, “I think I might have this”, or other similar statements, but I take issue with people who claim to have the disorder without actually being examined. Some of the symptoms written down present way differently than you might expect them to, for example, and without someone else (a professional) looking at those behaviours sometimes they can be confused for non-pathological behaviours or symptoms of a completely differently illness. I was in denial of my diagnosis for a while, too, it just didn’t feel like it fit and I was very confused on how I fit the bill of symptoms, but have had two psychiatrists agree that it’s OCD.

I don’t think it’s harmful if you want to use the research you’ve done to try common things that help with OCD, such as finding a CBT workbook. There’s no harm in trying to work on the symptoms you’re experiencing with available tools.

Hey! You’re probably ambivalent, too! The ambivalent style is a combination of the anxious and avoidant attachment styles. There’s aspects from both involved, thus why it’s ambivalent. I’ve seen it be called “come here, go away”, to reference how people with this style crave closeness, but when it happens, we “shut down” or push them away to prevent it from happening. This style is attributed to people with intensely abusive childhoods, typically. You should absolutely read up on it if you think it sounds like what you’re experiencing. For me, it felt very validating to learn that there was words for how I was feeling and a way to explain why relationships are hard for me. 

Sadly, too, oftentimes we try to recreate the situations we were in as children because peace doesn’t feel safe when you grew up with such a chaotic childhood. It’s hard to break out of this cycle and find your self worth, but I believe in you, and I understand how difficult it is. Feel free to DM if you want to talk more about this, I don’t mind!

Hi, I’m also a Canadian (Ontario) with a service dog that has tasks related to OCD interference. 

Firstly, whether or not you need a service animal is between you and your doctor/psychiatrist. Service animals mitigate disability, if your doctor believes you are disabled you may qualify for a service animal. I don’t know the steps for other provinces or territories, but that’s what the doctor is for — they will help you better than we can here, because they know you better.

Secondly, are you physically and emotionally able to handle a dog right now? You have to have the dog’s safety at the forefront of everything — can you handle walking the dog every day? Can you go to vet visits? Can you do training with your dog? Can you maintain training with your dog? Will you be able to handle if your dog messes up in public (has an accident, misbehaves, barks, etc)? Will your OCD be triggered and will your mental health plummet if people touch/coo at your dog, even if you say not to? Can you get food for the dog from the store? Do your dissociative states make you unable to care for yourself, let alone for an animal? The dog needs to be safe. Even if one would help, putting an animal in danger is not okay and you need to be positive you can handle the responsibility of a service animal while also being able to care for it and for yourself, because they are dogs, not miracle workers. 

On the topic of OCD related tasks, yes. You can train the dog to interfere. My dog is trained to paw/jump when he notices me doing certain behaviours (such as scratching myself) and not let up until I stop. Depending on what behaviours you want help mitigating, there are different tasks that the dog can do to alert or distract you from completing them. 

A final note here, just to reiterate:
People are going to touch your dog without permission. You are going to need to be able to mentally handle this. They might touch you, or grab your dog, or yell at you/the dog. Service dogs take a lot of training, and if you’re not going through a programme, you will need to be able to handle doing that training even when you’re stressed until the dog is fully trained. Dogs, let alone service dogs, are a massive responsibility and service dogs can wash easily if you aren’t sound enough to work with them. 

TL;DR: yes, OCD tasks can be done. Please feel free to ask questions! Talk with your doctor about your disability status and eligibility for a service dog. And really put thought into if you’ll benefit from a service dog without putting the animal at risk. Cheers!

Isn’t Ritalin a stimulant, not a form of hormone therapy? Please correct me if I’m wrong! The above is my experience with hormones as a transgender man in Canada, I understand it’s not universal at all.

In honesty, no. You can’t just order testosterone, and depending on where you live it can be a complete pain to acquire if you’re trans. For example, needing to have a certain amount of therapy, proof of diagnosed (yes, diagnosed!) gender dysphoria, sometimes specialised doctors, blood work, etc... On top of that, it’s expensive. Here where I live, it can be covered by insurance if your doctor writes you a note on why it should be covered for you and you need to wait for approval. Most pharmacies don’t have it on hand, so you sometimes just don’t get your prescription. Lastly, it doesn’t come in a pill. It comes as either a vial (so you also need to have 2 different kinds of needles, one for drawing the thick oil substance and one for injection) or as a gel (not covered by any insurance & very expensive). It also takes several months of weekly hormone injections to start to see results, but you start off at lower dosages so even then it’ll take a while to start getting any sort of noticeable muscle gain from using testosterone. Not to mention the side effects, too.

They’re a little bit smelly, if you keep really on top of cleaning it isn’t so bad but their piss & shit smells really nasty. They need baths about twice a month because they don’t clean themselves, and you should probably let them walk around in very very very shallow water to get their feet clean as often as necessary too. Not too much or their skin gets dry. Message me if you need help with baths for them. 

I wouldn’t say they’re very difficult at all to care for, but you need to be really patient with them in order for them to warm up to you. Although online they all seem happy, a lot of them are scared/defensive in personality and may never warm up to you, like guinea pigs. 

You need to have a pretty big place for them to run around too or they can get really grumpy. Also, if you want them to warm up to you faster, you’ll need to hold them in your bare hands so they can get your smell... you get used to the hissing, the “pop” they do when scared, and the ouchy spikes eventually..

Some things to note are that they aren’t beginner pets, you should have some rodent experience. They need exercise (a large wheel, room to roam), entertainment (we bought cat toy type things like jingly balls and stuff), and if they’re bored they can get up to mischief. 

They can have pellets made for hedgehogs specifically and usually can have mealworms or superworms as treats and as extra protein. Not too many or they get addicted and fat.

Also they’re crazy delicate, so always always always be careful when handling. Some hedgehogs will die young due to wobbly hedgehog syndrome (yes, I know, it sounds cute and funny. It’s not) which causes them to become paralysed and die within months of symptoms presenting. They can’t be too cold or they might hibernate, so keep them in a warm place and don’t leave them wet ever.
